newsitem.title: UK: Tin prices to recover strongly in 1997 - Wolff.
newsitem.headline: Tin prices to recover strongly in 1997 - Wolff.

text.p: Tin prices are set to rebound strongly in 1997, driven higher by a widening supply deficit, said William Adams, analyst at LME brokers Rudolf Wolff.
Addressing the London Metal Exchange (LME) metals seminar on Monday, Adams forecast three month tin prices to average at around $6,800 a tonne from current levels of around $6,050.
"For 1997 we are very bullish," Adams said.
"Our forecasts for 1997 are for prices to range between $6,000 and around $7,300," he added. "We think $5,900 is a low price."
Admas forecast a Western world supply deficit of 9,365 tonnes in 1997 up from a 1996 shortfall of 6,320 tonnes.
Refined output in the West was expected to rise to 152,300 tonnes in 1997 from 146,500 tonnes in 1996, while consumption was seen growing to 200,665 tonnes next year from 194,820 tonnes this year.
Former Eastern Bloc exports were pegged at 27,000 tonnes next year, down from 30,000 tonnes in 1996.
Sales from the Defence Logistics Agency (DLA) in the U.S. were expected to remain flat at 12,000 tonnes.
Adams said refined metal capacity would rise sharply over the period, but a lack of concentrate feed would mean that actual output growth would be slower.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see some closures among the toll smelters (because of the lack of mine output)," he said.
Adams said Chinese tin production in 1996 would be below year-ago levels because of flooding in producing regions and concentrate shortages.
Potential exports were down sharply because of the output problems and rising internal consumption, he added.
Despite this, low world prices had kept a lid on Chinese tin exports to the West.
"Watch out for a pick-up in Chinese exports if prices start to rise," Adams said, adding that around 5,000 tonnes could be ready for shipment in such a scenario.
Tin prices would benefit from growing markets, with the canning industry in Europe likely to continue to use more tin at the expense of aluminium.
The amount of tin in soldering is set to grow, while there are also potential growth markets in wine bottle tops, gunshot and chemicals.
"These new markets have the potential to have a large impact on tin consumption," Adams said.
